SUAS-012 — SuperUnicode Character Database

The structural counterpart of UAX #44: one verified binary image, one 16-byte range record, and a lookup that is one directory load, at most one index load, and one compare.

SUAS-012 (SUCD) is the twelfth SuperUnicode Architecture Standard and the structural counterpart of UAX #44, the Unicode Character Database. UAX #44 defines the database as a collection of text files, each with its own columns, its own range syntax, and its own defaults. SUCD keeps the data and closes the architecture around it: one binary image, a bounded lookup, and a partition the compiler must prove before it emits a byte.

A database defined as a folder of files has no architecture. It states no single definition of a record, offers no guarantee that two files agree about the same codepoint, declares no relationship between the human-readable form and the machine form, and bounds no query. Every implementation that wants a runtime table writes its own compiler, its own reconciliation rules, and its own bugs. SUCD makes the reconciliation a specified step instead of a tradition.

Why a binary image

Aspect UAX #44 SUCD
Definition A folder of text files One verified binary image, compiled from the files
Record shape Per-file columns One 16-byte range record, uniform across properties
Address space 17 planes, 21 bits 31 bits, 0x00000000–0x7FFFFFFF
Lookup Read the file, or build your own map Two-level directory, O(1)
Consistency Left to the implementer A partition, proven by the compiler
Defaults Per-file @missing lines One default record, Cn and no properties
Overlap Allowed and common Rejected by the verifier
Failure mode A file disagrees with another The verifier names the first defect

The character record

Every property, block and classification compiles into the same fixed record. A point is a range whose endpoints are equal, so there is no separate single-codepoint form for a caller to special-case.

typedef struct {
uint32_t first; /* inclusive range start */
uint32_t last; /* inclusive range end */
uint32_t property_mask; /* SUCD_PROP_* bits */
uint16_t general_category; /* sucd_general_category_t */
uint8_t script_id; /* SUAS-005 (SSP) */
uint8_t flags; /* SUCD_RECORD_* */
} sucd_record_t;

Seventeen property bits are assigned, one per property the published 0.1.0 files actually name, and the upper fifteen are reserved so that an unmasked bit is a detectable defect rather than an accident. The spellings are the files’ own: a compiler matches Unicode_Bridged, and the API returns Unicode_Bridged.

Source Properties
Props/PropList.txt Unicode_Bridged, Control_Plane, Printable, the four Diagnostic_*, Trap_Instruction, Sentinel_Value
Derived/DerivedCoreProperties.txt Alphabetic, Control
Props/BidiProps.txt LTR, RTL, ARABIC_AL, NEUTRAL, MIRRORED, WHITESPACE

The three-kinded page directory

The 31-bit space splits into 32 768 pages of 65 536 codepoints. Each directory slot is exactly one of three things, because the space is simultaneously enormous and empty in the middle and dense at the bottom.

Slot Kind Meaning
SUAS_SUCD_NO_PAGE Empty Every codepoint in the page is unassigned
SUAS_SUCD_UNIFORM_TAG | i Uniform Record i covers the whole page; no index load
anything else Dense Offset into the page’s per-codepoint uint16 index

The Native allocation is one range spanning more than two billion codepoints, so a dense table for it would cost 4 GiB; the ASCII page carries a dozen distinct bidirectional classifications, so a uniform slot cannot describe it. Three kinds let the Native plane pay one slot per page while ASCII pays one index, and the empty middle pays nothing at all.

Lookup and its cost

slot = directory[cp >> 16]
if slot == NO_PAGE → default record
if slot & UNIFORM_TAG → i = slot & 0x7FFFFFFF
else → i = dense[slot + (cp & 0xFFFF)]
r = records[i]
return (cp < r.first || cp > r.last) ? default : r
Operation Cost
suas_sucd_get_record O(1) — one directory load, ≤ one index load, one record load
suas_sucd_property_mask / _plane_of O(1)
suas_sucd_verify_image O(image extent) — one pass, no allocation
suas_sucd_range_form / _parse_range O(len) over a fixed line
suas_sucd_verify_schema_link O(1) expected — one SSRE lookup

The image stores no dense-index length. Its size, the fixed directory size and total_records determine the dense extent exactly, and a size that admits no exact layout is rejected — so there is no length field for a corrupt image to lie about.

Verification names the defect

A loader that rejects an image must be able to say which invariant failed. suas_sucd_verify_image returns the first of seventeen named outcomes: a bad magic, a wrong directory count, a record count over capacity, a size that is not a layout, a bad cursor flag, a reversed range, a codepoint past the space, a general category out of range, a reserved property bit, unordered records, overlapping records, a directory slot that names no record, a dense offset past the index, or a page that its uniform record does not actually cover.

Unordered and overlapping records are rejected outright, so the partition is an image property rather than a hope. A codepoint that is merely unassigned is not a failure at all: it receives the default record — Cn, no properties, the UNKNOWN script — because a database that answers “not assigned” is answering the question.

The published files are not a partition

The standard says so plainly. SUCSData.txt and Blocks.txt nest — the Native row swallows the traps and the Sentinel, and the control-plane block swallows the four diagnostic blocks. PropList.txt overlays Control_Plane on the Diagnostic_* ranges. BidiProps.txt overlaps and duplicates itself. And Traps.txt marks trap codepoints unassigned against the enclosing Native allocation.

Four range syntaxes coexist across the tree, so a compiler that reads only one convention silently drops most of the database; suas_sucd_range_form and suas_sucd_parse_range decode all four. The overlaps are resolved by the compiler, deterministically — narrower wins for nested ranges, and an explicit Bidirectional override wins over its enclosing range — and the result must still satisfy the partition before an image is written.

Numbering note

The seeding sketch was labelled SUAS-014; it is registered as SUAS-012, the number immediately after SUAS-011 (SCMS), which keeps the SUAS series contiguous with no reserved gaps. SUAS-014 is not used by this specification; SUAS-013, allocated afterwards, is SISR.

As with SIP, SSRE, SCMS, and SCSS, the brief named the reference layer “SUCA”; in this corpus SUCA is already the SuperUnicode Collation Algorithm (SUTS-001), so this standard names SUCD as the character database.

Reference implementation: include/suas/suas_sucd.h + src/suas/suas_sucd.c (freestanding C99, no heap), registered in suas_static and in the SSRE registry as a MANDATORY specification.

Source of truth: docs/suas/SUAS-012-sucd.md in the repository.
